opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important lessons we can take, and honestly one the field hasn't fully absorbed yet. If you watch a child playing with blocks, or an adult poking at a new piece of software, nobody hands them a scalar reward. They're not maximizing anything you could easily write down. Yet they come away with these rich, structured, causal models of how the thing works. What's driving that seems to be something more like curiosity, or a drive to compress and explain what they're seeing, a desire to have a theory that accounts for the data.

For program synthesis, I think that suggests a shift in what we treat as the objective. A lot of classical synthesis is very goal-directed: here's a specification, here are some input-output examples, find me a program that satisfies them. That's useful, but it's a narrow slice of what humans do. The more interesting setting is where the program *is* the model of the world. You see observations, and you're trying to write down a program that explains them, a generative model, a simulator, a theory. Then the "reward," to the extent there is one, is intrinsic. It's something like how well the program explains the data, traded off against how simple or elegant it is. That's basically a Bayesian or minimum-description-length view, and I think it fits remarkably well with how people seem to learn.

There's also a second piece, which is that people don't just passively fit models, they act to get informative data. They run little experiments. So I think program synthesis should be coupled with active learning: the system should ask which experiment would best disambiguate between the candidate programs it's considering. That's how you get efficient learning without anyone telling you what matters.

And third, people build up libraries of concepts over time. The abstractions you form in one domain make the next one easier. That's a lot of what motivated work like DreamCoder: the idea that you shouldn't just solve problems, you should be growing a vocabulary of reusable abstractions, and that vocabulary is itself learned without supervision, just from trying to explain more and more of your experience compactly.

So, put together, the picture I find compelling is a synthesis system that's an intrinsically motivated scientist: it proposes programs as theories, it runs experiments to test them, and it accumulates a library that makes future theorizing easier. And now that we have language models that give us really strong priors over code, I think that picture has become a lot more tractable than it was even a few years ago. The neural model gives you intuition about what programs are plausible, and the symbolic program gives you something that's interpretable, compositional, and generalizes in the systematic way human theories do.

r001.rationale: The response proposes curiosity and the drive to compress and explain observations as intrinsic motivations, and frames this through a Bayesian or minimum-description-length account.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose robustness across a range of possible reward functions; it focuses on learning without an externally specified reward.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that's one of the most important observations we have about human learning, and it's one that program synthesis has mostly ignored. If you look at the standard setup, we hand the system a specification: input-output examples, a reward, a test suite, something that tells it when it's done. But that's not how a child figures out how a toy works. They poke at it, they build a model of what the buttons do, what the moving parts are, and only much later, if ever, does a goal show up that uses that model. The modeling comes first, and the reward comes after, if at all.

So what I take from that is that we should be building systems that synthesize programs as explanations rather than as solutions. A program is a pretty good format for a world model. It's compositional, it's interpretable, and it can be edited and reused. If I learn a program that captures how this object behaves, I can later plug it into a planner, or compose it with other programs, or hand it to someone else. The reward-free part is really about what objective you're optimizing. Instead of task success, you're optimizing something like description length, or predictive accuracy, or how much surprise the model removes from your observations. Those are objectives that exist before any task is specified.

The other thing I'd say is that humans don't just build one model, they build a library. The abstractions you learn playing with blocks turn out to be useful when you're learning physics, or stacking dishes. In our work on library learning, like DreamCoder, the idea is that each program you write gives you candidate abstractions, and the useful ones get compressed into your language so the next problem is easier to express. That loop doesn't actually need a reward signal to drive it. It just needs a stream of experience and a pressure toward compression and reuse.

Where it gets interesting is the interaction with active exploration. If you're not being told what to do, you have to decide what to look at, and the right thing to look at is whatever your current models fail to explain. That's a very natural fit with program induction, because a program that fails on a particular input tells you very precisely where your understanding is missing. So I think the research agenda is roughly: learn programs as models, grow a library of abstractions from them, and let the gaps in those models drive what you explore next. Rewards can come later, and when they do, you've already got the representations to make the problem tractable.

r001.rationale: The response proposes modeling objectives such as description length and predictive accuracy, but does not propose theories of intrinsic motivation as an explanation for abstract model formation.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose robustness across a wide range of possible reward functions; it discusses learning models before rewards are specified.

astra-6.text:
I think it suggests that we’re missing something if we frame program synthesis entirely as solving a task with a specification somebody hands us. People build representations before they know exactly what those representations are going to be useful for. You can notice a pattern, invent a concept, or figure out how something works without getting an explicit reward for doing it.

For program synthesis, that raises the question of how a system could discover useful abstractions on its own. Instead of only asking, “Can I write a program that produces these outputs?”, we could also ask, “What reusable pieces make this collection of things easier to describe?” If several programs share some structure, maybe that structure should become a new function in your programming language. Then it becomes something you can use to think with when you encounter the next problem.

Compression gives us one possible signal for that. An abstraction is useful if it helps explain many examples economically. But I wouldn’t equate compression with the whole story of human learning. You also have to decide what to explore and which patterns are worth trying to understand.

So I’d like program synthesis systems that don’t just get better at searching within a fixed language. They should also learn the language they search in, and do some of that learning before a particular downstream task tells them what matters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses discovering abstractions and choosing what to explore, but does not propose normative theories of intrinsic motivation as an explanation.

r002.rationale: The response mentions learning before a downstream task specifies what matters, but does not propose robustness across a wide range of possible reward functions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it suggests that program synthesis should be about more than finding a program that maximizes some externally specified reward. People seem to build models because those models help them understand what they’re seeing, and those models can become useful for goals they haven’t encountered yet.

Imagine looking at a collection of objects and noticing that they’re arranged symmetrically. Nobody has to reward you for discovering symmetry. You can represent the scene more compactly, and that representation lets you predict missing pieces or imagine variations. In program synthesis terms, you’ve discovered a little program that explains the observations.

That motivates learning libraries of reusable abstractions alongside learning individual programs. You solve some problems, find structure shared across the solutions, and turn that structure into building blocks that make future problems easier. The language you’re synthesizing programs in should itself develop through experience.

Of course, saying there’s no explicit reward doesn’t mean there’s no learning signal. Prediction, compression, and reuse can all supply signals. The research question is how to make those signals produce abstractions that support later reasoning and learning, rather than just fitting the observations you already have.

r001.rationale: The response mentions model-building without explicit rewards and signals such as prediction, compression, and reuse, but does not propose normative theories of intrinsic motivation as an explanation.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose robustness across a wide range of possible reward functions; it discusses abstractions that help with future problems instead.
